input.subject: LibreSSL and OpenSSL separation in libpq to support 1.1.1 deprecation

verdict_reasoning: The goal has support in the thread, but the design is not agreed. maintenance-fit-1 is decisive: the patch copies about 1900 common lines, and nothing fails when a change reaches only one copy. Message #3 offers a shared file, and the thread has not settled it. demand-2, standards-compat-1 and standards-compat-2 are fixable points on order of work, build options and the USE_OPENSSL define.

brief.title: Split LibreSSL support out of the OpenSSL code into separate modules
brief.problem: Postgres supports LibreSSL through the OpenSSL code path, with ifdefs for API differences. LibreSSL stays on the 1.1.1-style API, so moving libpq and the backend to OpenSSL 3.0+ APIs after dropping 1.1.1 would add more ifdefs. The author calls the result unreadable and a CVE hazard; serverside SNI is already unavailable with LibreSSL for this reason.
brief.proposed_design: The patch copies the OpenSSL code into new be-secure-libressl.c and fe-secure-libressl.c and removes the compatibility ifdefs from both copies. It adds a separate build option and extends the SSL test infrastructure for LibreSSL. It is a PoC: autoconf support is untested and build documentation is missing.
user_visible_surface: Meson option ssl gains the choice 'libressl'; the description no longer lists only openssl.
A matching configure (autoconf) option for LibreSSL, whose name the material does not show.
New build define USE_LIBRESSL next to USE_OPENSSL, visible to code that checks pg_config.h.
author_claims: The patch adds or removes no features and changes no API usage.
Diffing the openssl and libressl files makes the differences easy to check.
Maintenance burden is not new, since LibreSSL is already supported and must be tested, but backpatching gets harder.
LibreSSL lacks the manpower to follow OpenSSL and will likely stay on the 1.1.1 API.
Serverside SNI for LibreSSL, planned for v20, needs this split to keep files readable.
brief.thread_state: Peter Eisentraut objects that most code is shared, so changes would be made and tested twice and the LibreSSL copy may degrade; Álvaro Herrera suggests a shared file for common routines. Jacob Champion and Michael Paquier support the split together with dropping OpenSSL 1.1.1 in v20, and the order of the two steps is open.
unclear: The material does not say whether the autoconf option is --with-ssl=libressl or something else.
The material does not say what happens with ssl=auto when both libraries are installed.
The patch does not say whether any buildfarm animals will cover the LibreSSL build.
The thread does not settle whether common code goes into a shared file, and the author rejects including a .c file.
The material does not give a minimum supported LibreSSL version.
Álvaro reports fe-secure-libressl.c may miss recent changes such as 7d45a6dc1974; the thread does not confirm it.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Add notBefore and notAfter to SSL cert info display"
prior_attempts.quote: LibreSSL didn't support ASN1_TIME_diff until OpenBSD 7.1, leaving the older OpenBSD animals in the buildfarm complaining.
prior_attempts.reason:
This reverts commit 6acb0a628eccab8764e0306582c2b7e2a1441b9b since
LibreSSL didn't support ASN1_TIME_diff until OpenBSD 7.1, leaving
the older OpenBSD animals in the buildfarm complaining.

Per plover in the buildfarm.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P5 reverted one feature because old LibreSSL lacked an API. This proposal changes no feature; it moves the LibreSSL differences into separate files.

objections.title: Two copies of about 1900 shared lines with no check against drift
objections.failure_scenario: A committer fixes a TLS bug or a security issue in be-secure-openssl.c and backpatches it. The same code in be-secure-libressl.c is left unchanged, and every test on OpenSSL builds passes. LibreSSL users keep the bug until someone diffs the two files by hand.
objections.argument: Message #3 counts 1889 common lines and only about 640 differing lines in the backend pair, and it reports that fe-secure-libressl.c may already miss 7d45a6dc1974 in the PoC itself. Message #4 says testing twice is not new, and that is true, but applying every change twice is new, and message #1 agrees backpatching gets harder. A missed change in the copy fails only if a LibreSSL buildfarm animal runs a test for it, and the patch names no such coverage.
objections.author_must_show: Which mechanism, such as a shared file for common routines or a required LibreSSL CI run, makes a change applied to only one copy fail loudly?

critic.reasoning: Message #4 answers the testing cost but concedes that applying changes twice is a real cost, and message #1 concedes harder backpatching. The thread has not settled the shared file from message #3, and the patch names no LibreSSL coverage.

objections.title: New USE_LIBRESSL define can silently drop SSL code in extensions
objections.failure_scenario: An extension that reads SSL connection details guards its code with `#ifdef USE_OPENSSL`, as is common today. Built against a v20 LibreSSL server, it compiles without error but leaves out its SSL code. Users see missing SSL information at run time, with no build error.
objections.argument: The brief lists USE_LIBRESSL as a new pg_config.h define next to USE_OPENSSL, and message #1 mentions `USE_OPENSSL || USE_LIBRESSL` checks. The touched files include no contrib module, so the proposal does not say how pgcrypto and sslinfo, which depend on OpenSSL, are enabled in a libressl build. The proposal also does not say whether USE_OPENSSL stays defined for LibreSSL builds, or what extension authors should test for.
objections.author_must_show: In a libressl build, is USE_OPENSSL still defined, are pgcrypto and sslinfo built, and what should out-of-tree code check?

critic.reasoning: The touched files include no contrib module, and the material does not say whether USE_OPENSSL stays defined in a libressl build. The author's claim that no features are removed depends on that answer for pgcrypto, sslinfo and out-of-tree code.

objections.title: Existing LibreSSL builds using ssl=openssl get no defined behavior
objections.failure_scenario: An OpenBSD packager or buildfarm owner keeps `--with-ssl=openssl` or `-Dssl=openssl` against LibreSSL, as works today, and upgrades to v20. The openssl files no longer carry the compatibility ifdefs, so the build fails late or compiles against APIs LibreSSL lacks. The packager finds out at build or run time.
objections.argument: Today LibreSSL is used through the openssl option, so every existing LibreSSL build script names `openssl`. The patch adds a `libressl` choice to meson_options.txt. The proposal does not say whether the openssl choice will detect LibreSSL and stop with a clear message, or pick libressl by itself. It also does not say which library `ssl=auto` picks when both are installed, and the autoconf spelling is not shown.
objections.author_must_show: What does a v20 build with ssl=openssl against LibreSSL headers do, and what does ssl=auto pick when both libraries are present?

precedents.title: Revert "Add notBefore and notAfter to SSL cert info display"

critic.reasoning: Message #1 lists meson discovery and autoconf as unfinished, and the material does not say what ssl=openssl does against LibreSSL headers or what ssl=auto picks. [P5] concerns a missing API in old LibreSSL and must not be used as support.

objections.title: The split has no payoff until OpenSSL 1.1.1 support is dropped
objections.failure_scenario: The split is committed for v20, but the OpenSSL 1.1.1 drop slips or is reduced in scope. The project then carries two near-identical TLS files with no 3.0+ API code to justify them, and every TLS backpatch to v20 has to be applied twice.
objections.argument: Message #4 says there is no point in the patch until 1.1.1 is deprecated, and message #1 offers to keep it rebased until a v3+ API is needed. Message #7 leaves the order of the two steps open. Serverside SNI for LibreSSL is the only concrete near-term user named, and it is planned work, not code.
objections.author_must_show: Has the OpenSSL 1.1.1 drop for v20 been agreed, and which committed or posted patch needs a 3.0+ API that the shared file cannot carry?

critic.reasoning: The author states the same condition in messages #1 and #4, but message #7 leaves the order open and prefers the split first. The material does not show that the 1.1.1 drop is agreed, so the scenario can happen.

refuted.title: Separate LibreSSL module has no stated minimum LibreSSL version
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer adds an API call such as the planned serverside SNI to be-secure-libressl.c and tests it on a current LibreSSL. Older OpenBSD animals in the buildfarm then fail to build, and the commit is reverted after the push.
refuted.argument: [P5] records a revert caused by a LibreSSL API that older OpenBSD releases did not have, and message #4 reports other reverts of the same kind. The commit message says LibreSSL support started with no minimum version, and the patch still does not set one. The split exists so the LibreSSL code can move at its own pace, so the lowest LibreSSL release it must build against needs to be decided.
refuted.author_must_show: Which minimum LibreSSL version will be-secure-libressl.c and fe-secure-libressl.c support, and which buildfarm animals will cover that floor?

precedents.title: Revert "Add notBefore and notAfter to SSL cert info display"

critic.reasoning: The Postgres installation documentation already states a minimum LibreSSL version, and the commit message says only that support began without one. The revert in [P5] predates that floor, and the same risk exists today with the shared file.

refuted.title: New USE_LIBRESSL define silently changes what extensions compile against
refuted.failure_scenario: An out-of-tree extension includes libpq-be.h and uses Port->ssl under #ifdef USE_OPENSSL. On a LibreSSL build, such as an OpenBSD package, pg_config.h now defines USE_LIBRESSL and not USE_OPENSSL, so the extension builds cleanly with its TLS code compiled out. Users find out only when the feature returns nothing at run time.
refuted.argument: Today a LibreSSL build defines USE_OPENSSL, and extension code relies on that. The patch adds USE_LIBRESSL next to it and touches libpq-be.h, libpq-int.h and pg_config.h.in. The TODO in message #1 already lists places that need USE_OPENSSL || USE_LIBRESSL, which shows that in-tree code needed changes too. The proposal does not say what extension authors should test for, or whether USE_OPENSSL stays defined on LibreSSL builds for compatibility.
refuted.author_must_show: On a LibreSSL build, which of USE_OPENSSL, USE_LIBRESSL and USE_SSL are defined, and what should out-of-tree code that reads Port->ssl test for?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2, which covers the same USE_OPENSSL guard problem and also the contrib modules.

refuted.title: Duplicated TLS code lets security fixes miss the LibreSSL copy
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer fixes a certificate-verification or channel-binding bug in fe-secure-openssl.c and tests it with OpenSSL only. The same bug remains in fe-secure-libressl.c, so clients built with LibreSSL keep connecting with weaker checks. Nobody notices until a separate report against an OpenBSD build, possibly after a security release has shipped.
refuted.argument: The patch copies about 1900 common lines into a second file, as Álvaro counted in message #3, and nothing makes a change to one copy fail when the other is left alone. Message #3 already suspects fe-secure-libressl.c lacks a recent change, and message #2 predicts the copy will degrade. The author argues that ifdefs are a CVE hazard, but two diverging copies are also a hazard, and back branches keep a single file, so each security backpatch must be redone two ways in master.
refuted.author_must_show: How will a security fix to the shared TLS logic reach both copies, for example through a shared common file, and what test or buildfarm animal fails if it does not?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which states the same drift between the two copies with the line counts from message #3.

refuted.title: Extract the shared code first, before forking the files
refuted.failure_scenario: The full copy is committed in v20. The shared file that message #3 suggests is never written, so every later TLS patch, including the planned LibreSSL SNI work, touches two near-identical files for the whole life of the release branches.
refuted.argument: Message #6 accepts a split into a common file plus library-specific files, but the PoC copies whole files and leaves that step for later. A series that first moves library-neutral routines into be-secure-common.c or a shared OpenSSL/LibreSSL file could be committed and judged on its own. Then the size of the real difference would decide whether a full fork is still needed, which is the open question in message #2.
refuted.author_must_show: After moving identical routines into a shared file, how many lines would remain different between the OpenSSL and LibreSSL files on each side?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1: the failure scenario is the same drift cost, and the shared file is already the remedy that objection asks about.

refuted.title: USE_LIBRESSL next to USE_OPENSSL may break code that tests USE_OPENSSL
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension that guards its TLS code with #ifdef USE_OPENSSL is built against a LibreSSL-configured server. The guard is now false, so the extension builds without its TLS support and gives no error. The user finds out when the feature is missing at run time.
refuted.argument: The brief lists a new pg_config.h define, USE_LIBRESSL, and message #1 plans to replace USE_OPENSSL || USE_LIBRESSL with USE_SSL in core. The proposal does not say whether USE_OPENSSL stays defined for LibreSSL builds, or what the ssl_library setting and the libpq SSL library attribute report afterwards. Today both values are the same for the two libraries.
refuted.author_must_show: For a LibreSSL build, is USE_OPENSSL still defined, and what do ssl_library and the libpq SSL library attribute report compared with today?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. Its added question about what ssl_library reports can be asked under that objection.

refuted.title: No evidence of LibreSSL users large enough to justify a second copy
refuted.failure_scenario: After the split, every TLS fix or CVE patch in be-secure-openssl.c and fe-secure-openssl.c also has to land in the LibreSSL copy and be backpatched there. A committer who skips that step leaves the LibreSSL build behind, as message #3 suspects already happened with 7d45a6dc1974. Users find out from a bug report or a security advisory.
refuted.argument: Message #1 names two choices, deprecating LibreSSL or splitting it out, and picks the split because the author does not like deprecation. The thread gives no count of LibreSSL users, no packagers who depend on it, and no -general or -bugs reports. Message #1 also says LibreSSL lacks the manpower to keep up, so the duplicated code would serve a library that is expected to stagnate. All contributors pay the cost of the duplication, while only LibreSSL builds gain from it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which platforms or distributions ship Postgres built against LibreSSL today, and about how many users would lose TLS support if LibreSSL were deprecated?

precedents.title: Support for NSS as a libpq TLS backend

critic.reasoning: LibreSSL is already supported and buildfarm tested, so the patch adds no new user group, and the alternative is removing existing support. [P4] concerned adding a new library, and three TLS-area committers in the thread prefer the split to deprecation.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds USE_LIBRESSL to pg_config.h and changes libpq-be.h, which extensions that test USE_OPENSSL compile against.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The patch duplicates the TLS code of backend and libpq, so a security fix must reach two files.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Message #1 says the split makes backpatching harder, since back branches keep one file and master has two.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Two near-identical file pairs, a second build option and LibreSSL test infrastructure need care in every later TLS change.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which mechanism, such as a shared file for common routines or a required LibreSSL CI run, makes a change applied to only one copy fail loudly?
Has the OpenSSL 1.1.1 drop for v20 been agreed, and which posted patch needs a 3.0+ API that the shared file cannot carry?
In a libressl build, is USE_OPENSSL still defined, are pgcrypto and sslinfo built, and what should out-of-tree code check?
What does a v20 build with ssl=openssl against LibreSSL headers do, and what does ssl=auto pick when both libraries are installed?
Does fe-secure-libressl.c contain the change from 7d45a6dc1974, which message #3 suspects is missing?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the TLS code in libpq and the backend, and the build system, must own it. Daniel Gustafsson wrote the patch, and Peter Eisentraut and Álvaro Herrera reviewed the approach.
committability.liability: The owner signs for keeping two TLS file pairs in step on master for as long as LibreSSL is supported, and for backpatches from two files into single-file back branches.
committability.author_follow_up: The author offers in message #1 to keep the patch rebased, plans LibreSSL SNI work for v20, and moved the entry to the next CommitFest in October 2026.

priority.reason: Only LibreSSL builds gain directly, though the split also clears the way for OpenSSL 3.0+ APIs. The patch is a PoC of about 143 KiB, mostly copied code, and the thread must first choose between a full copy and a shared file.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the real size of the difference between the file pairs and the behaviour of the build discovery are unchecked. Only 3 of 9 thread messages were visible.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: OpenSSL 3.0.0 compatibility
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch series prepares Postgres for OpenSSL 3.0.0: it replaces deprecated API calls, moves test keys from DES to AES256 and makes pgcrypto load the legacy provider or the OpenSSL config file. It also documents that DES and Blowfish in pgcrypto need the legacy provider enabled in openssl.cnf.
precedents_retrieved.objection: OpenSSL 3.0.0 was still in alpha, and its error messages and pgcrypto behaviour kept changing between snapshots. Michael Paquier proposed setting the work aside until upstream reached at least a beta with stable APIs. Peter Eisentraut noted that no patch was still pending because most of the work had moved to other threads, and the author withdrew the entry to wait for 3.0.0 to ship.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
What if we just waited and
revisited this stuff during the next dev cycle, once there is at least
a beta, meaning mostly stable APIs?

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid mixing custom and OpenSSL BIO functions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the Postgres custom BIO, which mixed custom read/write functions with OpenSSL socket BIO functions, with a standalone custom BIO_METHOD that has its own ctrl callback. It also switches back from BIO_get_app_data to BIO_get_data.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Andres Freund asked which BIO_ctrl operations must be supported and raised naming and BIO_TYPE_DESCRIPTOR questions. The author posted a revised patch on 2024-02-21, and no later message explains the withdrawal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support for NSS as a libpq TLS backend
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds NSS, with its NSPR runtime, as a second TLS backend for libpq and the server, next to OpenSSL. It adds new settings for the NSS certificate database, splits the SSL TAP tests into per-backend modules, and covers pgcrypto and cryptohash code as well.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it as rejected after Robert Haas and Andres Freund raised objections, which he counted as a -1 late in the cycle. The objections shown concern NSS's long-term maintenance: Mozilla had removed the NSS and NSPR documentation from MDN, and curl and OpenLDAP were dropping NSS support. Stephen Frost argued that NSS is still maintained, but the patch was not revived.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: For the record, I do like the idea of adding NSS, but I am concerned about its long-term maintenance, we you explained.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support for NSS as TLS backend
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds NSS (with the NSPR runtime) as a second TLS backend for libpq and the server, next to OpenSSL, using an NSS certificate database instead of PEM files on disk. It also refactors the SSL TAP tests into per-library modules and moves other crypto users such as SCRAM and cryptohash onto NSS.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned it because it was still premature for integration and still had bugs, such as a failing DN mapping test found while rebasing v35. Reviewers had also found that NSS keeps global state that libpq cannot control: the first context becomes the default database, SECMOD_OpenUserDB duplicates slots, and implicit NSPR initialization is not thread-safe. So libpq would need its own locks, refcounts and an initialization API like PQinitOpenSSL().
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
For now, I have marked this patch set as returned with feedback as it
is still premature for integration, and there are still bugs in it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support tls-exporter as channel binding for TLSv1.3
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds tls-exporter (RFC 9266) as a SCRAM channel binding type, using SSL_export_keying_material(). It adds a libpq connection parameter channel_binding_type and the environment variable PGCHANNELBINDINGTYPE, with tls-server-end-point as the default.
precedents_retrieved.objection: OpenSSL 1.0.1 support and the safety rules for TLS before 1.3 (extended master secret, no renegotiation) made the patch grow in complexity. It also hit an old unsolved problem: client and server cannot negotiate which channel binding type to use. Michael Paquier suggested dropping tls-server-end-point from the backend, but Jacob Champion noted that proxy TLS termination needs it. The author then deferred the feature until a way to negotiate the binding type exists.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: For that, I would think tls-server-end-point is an important feature.

precedents_retrieved.title: libpq: Support for Apple Secure Transport SSL library
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add Apple Secure Transport as a second TLS library for libpq and the backend on macOS, next to OpenSSL, with an ssl_library GUC that reports the library in use. Certificates and keys load from PEM files or from macOS Keychains, which a new keychain parameter and a "keychain:" prefix on sslcert select.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback after the last patch set stopped applying (the SSL test refactoring was one cause) and the author had not replied for a week. He also reported a likely crash with SCRAM channel binding and asked for stub functions, because macOS does not expose the TLS finished message. Open work also remained on CRL support, Keychain passphrase handling and the documentation.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This last comment is from last week, so I am marking the patch as returned with feedback. This also needs more thoughts for channel binding support with SCRAM.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Change SHA2 implementation based on OpenSSL to use EVP digest routines"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Change SHA2 implementation based on OpenSSL to use EVP digest routines"
Reverted commit(s): Change SHA2 implementation based on OpenSSL to use EVP digest routines
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit e21cbb4, as the switch to EVP routines requires a
more careful design where we would need to have at least our wrapper
routines return a status instead of issuing an error by themselves to
let the caller do the error handling.  The memory handling was also
incorrect and could cause leaks in the backend if a failure happened,
requiring most likely a callback to do the necessary cleanup as the only
clean way to be able to allocate an EVP context requires the use of an
allocation within OpenSSL.  The potential rework of the wrappers also
impacts the fallback implementation when not building with OpenSSL.

Originally, prairiedog has reported a compilation failure, but after
discussion with Tom Lane this needs a better design.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h"
Reverted commit(s): libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 728f86fec65537eade8d9e751961782ddb527934.

The signal handling was a few bricks shy of a load in that commit,
which made the walreceiver non-responsive to SIGTERM while it was
waiting for the connection to be established. That prevented a standby
from being promoted.

Since it was non-essential refactoring, let's revert it to make v16
work the same as earlier releases. I reverted it in 'master' too, to
keep the branches in sync. The refactoring was a good idea as such,
but it needs a bit more work. Once we have developed a complete patch
with this issue fixed, let's re-apply that to 'master'.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid use deprecated Windows Memory API
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Alvaro Herrera, Daniel Gustafsson, Michael Paquier
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces LocalAlloc/LocalFree calls in Postgres Windows code with HeapAlloc/HeapFree on the default process heap. The author cited Microsoft documentation that recommends the heap functions for new applications.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers found no benefit: the code is not performance-sensitive, LocalAlloc is not deprecated, and Microsoft's own documentation calls the choice a matter of personal preference. Alvaro Herrera judged the patch useless and the new code less clean, and Michael Paquier recommended rejection, citing Daniel's and Alvaro's arguments.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I was looking at this thread, and echoing Daniel's and Alvaro's
arguments, I don't quite see why this patch is something we need.

precedents_retrieved.title: macOS Secure Transport SSL Support
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds Apple Secure Transport as an alternative TLS library to OpenSSL on macOS, for both frontend and backend. It loads certificates and keys from PEM files or macOS Keychains, and adds Keychain-specific libpq parameters and GUCs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: In November 2018 the v11 patch failed "make -C ssl check" with a pg_ctl bailout, and the reviewer asked for an updated version. The author did not reply for about two months, so the entry was returned with feedback. Documentation, CRL file support, channel binding and contrib/sslinfo support were also still missing.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This has not been answered yet, and a couple of months have gone by,
so I am marking the patch as returned with feedback.

roaster_notes.note: The NSS and Secure Transport entries ([P4], [P6], [P8], [P12]) added new TLS libraries and stopped for reasons specific to those libraries or to stalled patches. This proposal splits a library that is already supported, so those reasons do not apply.
From the standards angle, the SQL surface, catalogs, pg_dump and psql are unchanged. Only the build options and the pg_config.h define are user-facing.
Beyond the build define, the proposal touches no on-disk format, WAL, catalog or replication state, and it does not change the TLS behaviour on the wire.
Apart from the risk of drift between the duplicated TLS files, the split adds no privilege, role or exposure change. It is a build-time choice of library with no new features.
Objections found; the split's goal has support from Jacob Champion and Michael Paquier, so these concern the design and its cost, not the aim.

This is an internal restructuring of the TLS code, so no existing feature, extension or external tool could stand in for it; the status quo is the shared OpenSSL file with ifdefs. Whether to split fully, use a shared common file as in message #3, or keep the ifdefs is a design question for other angles.

The work is aimed at developers and maintainability, and three committers in the thread support it. My objections ask for evidence of LibreSSL demand and for a firm 1.1.1 decision. They do not reject the idea.
